extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially science fiction/fantasy writers and those writing for younger readers) interested in developing and using technology in stories
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for developing, presenting, and using science and technology in speculative fiction: how to research and extrapolate tech, adapt it to audience and character needs, and use it as metaphor, conflict, or plot device without drowning the story in needless detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the implications of the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the implications of the technology; consider what effects it will have in the world of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "I want to look at the implications of the technology, but I don’t want to be the guy who thinks that the war is going to end in a week..." Example anti-pattern: the WWI machine-gun fallacy (assuming a tech's obvious quantitative effect yields immediate, simplistic social outcomes). Use historical parallels (how tech changed warfare) to inform plausible social consequences rather than naive extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider pace of technological change vs societal adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take into account that technology can change faster than societies learn how to use it; this affects plausible short-term outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "World War I is one of those really interesting moments where the technology changed faster than our ability to understand how to use that technology changed." Use this tension to create believable confusion, misapplication, or transitional chaos in your story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt current technology forward (plausible extrapolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When guessing about the future, adapt present technologies forward in believable ways instead of inventing arbitrary devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an eye on current tech (Wired, DARPA, news) and extrapolate: e.g., pairing Mars one-way-trip social dynamics with 3D printing to solve logistical problems. Use real projects/articles as seeds for plausible future tech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make technology accessible and palatable to your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Present technology at a level that your target readers will find understandable and engaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Take the technology, but make it accessible and palatable." For younger audiences simplify exposition, emphasize wonder/fun, and avoid technical language that alienates readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground tech in real science when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use real scientific principles as a basis for the tech you show, especially if you want a sense of verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan's Zero G example: use real science (zero gravity, spacewalks, freeze-dried food) in ways that feel fun and plausible. Real science can inspire set-pieces and constraints that generate interesting situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on character needs when deploying technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure any technology in the story relates directly to what characters want or need; technology should serve character-driven goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Whatever the technology does has to relate to what the character wants." Use tech as a mechanism to create or resolve stakes (e.g., survival, rescue, personal goals) rather than as an isolated cool gadget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology as metaphor, MacGuffin, or source of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology can be a symbolic device, central plot object, or the engine of conflict and thematic exploration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Harrison Bergeron (technology as social metaphor), Black Mirror's 'Nosedive' (social-credit tech as critique), use the tech to explore corporate power, consumerism, identity, or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit technical detail; include only what's necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overwhelming readers with minutiae—give enough detail to support the premise and character action, no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Not too many details... however the technology can help the character." Anti-pattern: Andy Weir's book can bog some readers down with too much detail; the film succeeds by focusing on how tech serves the character. Provide functional detail that aids plot and character understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate who created the technology and embedded biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the creators' perspectives and built-in assumptions—their values shape how the technology behaves and whom it benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Look at who created it and what biases or what kind of flavor they are adding to it..." Example: Facebook was built by a college sophomore and encodes college-age priorities into social interaction design. Use creator bias to generate social effects or ethical tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagine failures, abuses, and edge-cases (what could go wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively brainstorm ways the technology can fail, be misused, or be pushed to extremes to generate conflict and plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework: find a new technology and "imagine how it could go wrong"—jot down potential conflicts and extreme uses. Failures and edge-cases often yield the richest dramatic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed stories from current tech practices (organic idea generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for story ideas that grow naturally out of technologies and practices we already have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: robots that build other robots leading to 'robot wranglers' on Mars—find the logical cultural or occupational continuations of current tech to create fresh story premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust scientific rigor to the needs of the series or story
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how 'hard' the science should be for a given book or series and be consistent where it matters for reader expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan notes starting with a hard-SF first book and then loosening rigor in later volumes; match level of detail and accuracy to genre expectations and narrative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technology to reveal character motivation and resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Let characters' interactions with technology demonstrate their drives, resourcefulness, and growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Watney example: technology and problem-solving reveal will to survive; use tech-based challenges to show rather than tell character traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use media about real science as research and inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consume documentaries, specialist periodicals, and genre-adjacent media to harvest believable details and unusual facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: read Wired, DARPA reports, watch Forensic Files (for forensic science inspiration). Such sources provide concrete, often surprising hooks—e.g., forensic geology or bugs in radiators—that can become plot elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider ubiquity and economics of tech for setting plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for how cheap, common, or widespread a technology is when worldbuilding (it changes what post-disaster or everyday life looks like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: very cheap solar lights mean post-apocalyptic settings after ~2020 should plausibly feature constant lighting unless authors explain otherwise. Economics and adoption rates alter plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize thematic or metaphorical truth over literal prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable—and often valuable—to be 'wrong' about future specifics if the technology serves a thematic or metaphorical truth about the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "You don’t read [Harrison Bergeron] and say, 'Oh, he got it wrong.'" Use speculative tech to explore contemporary concerns even if details don't come to pass.
